title: Cambodia
capsule: The post-Angkorian middle period of Cambodia (c. 1431–1863, here bounded to 1700–1803) saw the Khmer court relocated to the Phnom Penh region after Ayutthayan forces sacked Angkor in 1431, and the kingdom progressively squeezed between the expansionist Siamese and Vietnamese states. Through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Khmer rulers alternated between seeking Vietnamese or Siamese protection, often installing rival claimants who drew in outside armies; the Mekong Delta (Prey Nokor/Saigon) passed definitively to Nguyen lords by 1698. By 1800 Cambodia retained only its rump heartland along the middle Mekong and Tonle Sap, and its court at Udong functioned largely as a vassal of whichever regional power held current military advantage. French protectorate negotiations in 1863 ended this precarious position.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Cambodia's territorial extent in this period is poorly documented; boundaries fluctuated continuously with military fortunes and no formal delimitation with Siam or Vietnam was established, making any cartographic representation approximate.
